bib.title: Think Stats, Chapter 6: Operations on distributions

question: How do you describe asymmetry, and how do distributions combine under sums, linear maps and maxima, leading to the normal distribution and the Central Limit Theorem?
contributions: Skewness g1 and Pearson's median skewness gp
Random variables as generator objects; PDF vs CDF
Convolution gives the distribution of a sum
Closure of the normal under linear maps and sums; Central Limit Theorem with caveats

results.claim: Sample skewness is g1 = m3/m2^(3/2), where m2 is the mean squared deviation and m3 the mean cubed deviation.
results.setup: Definition for a sample x_i, i=1..n, mean mu.

results.claim: Pearson's median skewness gp = 3(mean - median)/sigma is robust to outliers, unlike g1.
results.setup: Any sample; robust means less vulnerable to outliers.
results.quote: This statistic is robust, which means that it is less vulnerable to the effect of

results.claim: Sum of two independent exponentials with the same lambda is Erlang with k=2, PDF lambda^2 z e^(-lambda z).
results.setup: Convolution of PDFs, integral from 0 to z.
results.quote: This, it turns out, is the PDF of an Erlang distribution with parameter k = 2

results.claim: Normal is closed under linear transformation: X' = aX+b gives N(a mu + b, a^2 sigma^2); sums of independent normals give N(muX+muY, sigmaX^2+sigmaY^2).
results.setup: X, Y normal (independence is implied by the convolution derivation, not stated here).
results.quote: The normal distribution has this property

results.claim: CLT: the sum of n values with mean mu and sd sigma is approximately N(n mu, n sigma^2).
results.setup: Independent, same distribution (can be relaxed), finite mean and variance; most Pareto excluded.
results.quote: the distribution of the sum is approximately N (nµ, nσ2)

results.claim: Convergence speed under the CLT depends on skewness: exponential sums converge at small n, lognormal sums do not.
Exercise data: BRFSS male heights roughly normal with mu=178 cm, sigma^2=59.4 cm.
results.setup: Exercise 6.6, US men; female mu=163, sigma^2=52.8. Variance is printed with unit cm as in the text.
results.quote: µ = 178 cm and σ2 = 59.4 cm for men
results.note: unit of variance printed as cm, likely cm^2

results.claim: Survey figure cited for illusory superiority: more than 80% of respondents think they are better than the average driver.
results.setup: 'in some surveys'; logically impossible for median, possible for mean.

limits: Short textbook chapter; no empirical results, claims are asserted not proven (CLT stated without proof or rate, e.g. Berry-Esseen).
Independence of X and Y in the convolution is used but not stated explicitly.
Exercises depend on thinkstats.com datasets and code (gini.py, Pmf.py); Python 2-era code, and the Sum class snippet is buggy (missing self).
Gumbel/extreme-value convergence of the maximum is mentioned, not derived.
practices: Avoid computing sample skewness g1 when outliers exist; compare mean and median or use Pearson's gp instead (Sec 6.1).
Do not evaluate a PDF at a point expecting a probability; integrate, or difference the CDF (Sec 6.3).
Estimate a sum's distribution by sampling Sum objects when no closed form exists, accepting inefficiency and inexactness (Sec 6.4).
Check CLT caveats (independence, finite variance, skewness) before assuming a sum is normal (Sec 6.6).
For products, look at the log of the products (Ex 6.14 hint).

terms.definition: A characteristic of a distribution; intuitively, it is a measure of how asymmetric the distribution is.
A statistic is robust if it is relatively immune to the effect of outliers.
An object that represents a random process.
A value generated by a random process.
Probability density function, the derivative of a continuous CDF.
An operation that computes the distribution of the sum of values from two distributions.
"The supreme law of Unreason," according to Sir Francis Galton, an early statistician.
